subject: psychology_ib
source: IB Diploma Programme Psychology guide (first assessment 2027): content (biological, cognitive, sociocultural approaches, research methodology), contexts (health and well-being, human development), concepts and classic studies; no Polish core curriculum for this subject

items.question: Which research method manipulates an independent variable to measure its effect on a dependent variable?
items.explanation: Only an experiment with random allocation allows a cause-and-effect conclusion.

items.text: In an experiment, the variable the researcher deliberately manipulates is the {{independent}} variable.
items.explanation: The dependent variable (DV) is what is measured as a result.

items.question: What is the variable that is measured as the outcome of an experiment called?
items.explanation: Changes in the DV are assumed to be caused by changes in the IV.

items.question: What kind of study compares pre-existing groups (e.g. men vs women) because the researcher cannot manipulate the independent variable?
items.explanation: Without random allocation to conditions, causation cannot be firmly established.

items.question: Name the sampling technique in which every member of the target population has an equal chance of being selected.
items.explanation: Random sampling reduces researcher bias but is rarely practical.

items.question: Which sampling technique selects participants simply because they are easily available (e.g. students in the researcher's class)?
items.explanation: It is quick and cheap, but the sample may not represent the population.

items.text: In {{snowball}} sampling, existing participants recruit further participants from among their acquaintances.
items.explanation: Useful for hard-to-reach populations, e.g. drug users.

items.question: Which research method measures the relationship between two variables without manipulating either of them?
items.explanation: Correlation shows association, not causation.

items.question: Which ethical principle requires that participants are told what the study involves and agree to take part?
items.explanation: For minors, consent is obtained from parents or guardians.

items.question: What is the procedure, carried out after a study, in which participants are told its true aims and any deception is revealed?
items.explanation: Debriefing should also make sure participants leave in the same state as they arrived.

items.text: The ethical right of participants to leave a study at any time without penalty is the right to {{withdraw}}.
items.explanation: Participants may also withdraw their data after the study.

items.question: What type of validity refers to how well the findings of a study generalise to real-life settings?
items.explanation: Artificial laboratory tasks often have low ecological validity.

items.question: What do we call a variable other than the independent variable that may have affected the dependent variable?
items.explanation: Confounding variables threaten the internal validity of an experiment.

items.question: What is the term for participants changing their behaviour because they have guessed the aim of the study?
items.explanation: Deception or a single-blind design can reduce demand characteristics.

items.question: Which research method is an in-depth investigation of a single person or a small group over time?
items.explanation: Patient HM is a famous example of a case study in psychology.

items.text: Using several methods, researchers or data sources to check that findings agree is called {{triangulation}}.
items.explanation: Triangulation increases the credibility of qualitative research.

items.question: What is the term for the brain's ability to change its structure and connections in response to experience?
items.explanation: Learning a skill, e.g. juggling, increases grey matter in related brain areas.

items.question: Which brain structure is essential for forming new long-term memories?
items.explanation: Damage to the hippocampus (as in patient HM) causes anterograde amnesia.

items.question: Which brain structure is primarily involved in processing fear and other emotional responses?
items.explanation: The amygdala is part of the limbic system.

items.question: What are the chemical messengers that carry a signal from one neuron to the next across the synapse?
items.explanation: Examples include dopamine, serotonin and acetylcholine.

items.question: Which neurotransmitter is most associated with reward, motivation and pleasure?
items.explanation: Addictive drugs increase dopamine activity in the brain's reward pathway.

items.question: Which neurotransmitter is strongly involved in learning and memory formation in the hippocampus?
items.explanation: Drugs that block acetylcholine receptors impair memory.

items.text: The tiny gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters travel is the {{synapse}}.
items.explanation: Neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the next neuron.

items.question: What do we call a chemical messenger released by a gland into the bloodstream?
items.explanation: Hormones act more slowly than neurotransmitters but their effects last longer.

items.question: Which hormone, often called the stress hormone, is released by the adrenal glands during prolonged stress?
items.explanation: Chronically high cortisol can impair memory and the immune system.

items.question: Which hormone is linked to social bonding, trust and mother-infant attachment?
items.explanation: Oxytocin is released during childbirth, breastfeeding and physical touch.

items.question: What kind of study compares identical and fraternal twins to estimate the genetic contribution to a trait?
items.explanation: Higher similarity in identical than fraternal twins suggests a genetic influence.

items.question: What is the term for the proportion of variation in a trait within a population that can be attributed to genetic differences?
items.explanation: A heritability of 0.5 means about half of the variation is linked to genes.

items.question: Which brain-imaging technique shows brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow?
items.explanation: fMRI has good spatial resolution but is indirect: it measures blood oxygen, not neurons.

items.question: What is the term for a mental framework of prior knowledge that organises how we interpret new information?
items.explanation: Schemas help us process information quickly but can distort memory.

items.question: Which memory model (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968) proposes sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory as separate stores?
items.explanation: Information passes from store to store through attention and rehearsal.

items.text: According to the multi-store model, information is kept in short-term memory and transferred to long-term memory through {{rehearsal}}.
items.explanation: Short-term memory holds about 7 items for up to about 30 seconds without rehearsal.

items.question: In Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model, which component stores verbal and auditory information?
items.explanation: It consists of a phonological store and an articulatory rehearsal process.

items.question: In the working memory model, which component holds visual and spatial information?
items.explanation: It lets you picture a route while listening to directions.

items.text: In the working memory model, the {{central executive}} directs attention and coordinates the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad.
items.explanation: Baddeley later added the episodic buffer, which integrates information from the subsystems.

items.question: Which type of long-term memory stores personal experiences and events, such as your last birthday?
items.explanation: Semantic memory stores facts; procedural memory stores skills.

items.question: In Kahneman's dual-process model, which system is fast, automatic and intuitive?
items.explanation: System 1 is efficient but prone to cognitive biases.

items.text: In the dual-process model, slow, effortful and analytical thinking is called {{System 2}} thinking.
items.explanation: System 2 is used for difficult calculations and careful decisions.

items.question: What is the name of the cognitive bias that makes us seek out and remember information that supports what we already believe?
items.explanation: Confirmation bias is one reason why people hold on to false beliefs.

items.question: Which heuristic leads people to judge how likely an event is by how easily examples come to mind?
items.explanation: After seeing news about plane crashes, people overestimate the risk of flying.

items.question: Which cognitive bias describes relying too heavily on the first piece of information offered when making a decision?
items.explanation: An initial price acts as an anchor that shapes later judgments of value.

items.text: Memory is {{reconstructive}}: we rebuild memories from schemas and fragments rather than replaying an exact recording.
items.explanation: Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study showed how schemas distort recall.

items.question: Which theory by Tajfel and Turner states that part of our self-concept comes from the groups we belong to?
items.explanation: Group membership boosts self-esteem through positive comparison with out-groups.

items.text: Social identity theory describes three processes: social {{categorisation}}, social identification and social comparison.
items.explanation: We categorise people, identify with our in-group and compare it favourably with out-groups.

items.text: Favouring members of one's own group over members of other groups is called {{in-group}} favouritism.
items.explanation: Tajfel's minimal group studies showed in-group favouritism even in arbitrary groups.

items.question: Which theory by Bandura explains learning through observing and imitating others?
items.explanation: Attention, retention, reproduction and motivation are needed for observational learning.

items.question: What is the term for changing one's behaviour or opinions to match those of a group?
items.explanation: Asch's line study is the classic demonstration of conformity.

items.question: What type of social influence makes people conform because they want to be liked and accepted by the group?
items.explanation: This often produces public compliance without private agreement.

items.question: What type of social influence makes people conform because they believe the group has better information?
items.explanation: It is strongest in ambiguous or difficult situations.

items.question: Which of Hofstede's cultural dimensions contrasts personal goals and independence with loyalty to the group?
items.explanation: The USA scores high on individualism; many East Asian countries score high on collectivism.

items.question: Which of Hofstede's cultural dimensions describes how much a society accepts unequal distribution of power?
items.explanation: In high power-distance cultures, hierarchy is accepted without question.

items.text: A {{stereotype}} is a generalised, often oversimplified belief about the characteristics of a group of people.
items.explanation: Stereotypes can lead to prejudice and discrimination.

items.question: What is the process by which people adopt the culture of a new country while keeping or losing their heritage culture?
items.explanation: Berry described four strategies: integration, assimilation, separation and marginalisation.

items.question: What is the process by which children learn the norms and values of their own culture?
items.explanation: Enculturation happens through parents, peers, school and media.

items.text: The learned, shared rules of behaviour that members of a culture are expected to follow are called cultural {{norms}}.
items.explanation: Norms for personal space, eye contact or punctuality differ between cultures.

items.text: Piaget's first stage of cognitive development, from birth to about 2 years, is the {{sensorimotor}} stage.
items.explanation: In this stage the child develops object permanence.

items.question: In which of Piaget's stages (about 2-7 years) do children use symbols and language but think egocentrically?
items.explanation: Preoperational children fail conservation tasks.

items.question: In which of Piaget's stages (about 7-11 years) can children think logically about concrete objects and pass conservation tasks?
items.explanation: Abstract, hypothetical reasoning only appears in the formal operational stage.

items.question: What is Piaget's term for fitting new information into an existing schema?
items.explanation: Calling a zebra a 'horse' is assimilation.

items.text: When a child changes an existing schema to fit new information, Piaget called this {{accommodation}}.
items.explanation: Learning that a zebra is not a horse requires accommodation.

items.question: What is Vygotsky's term for the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from a more skilled person?
items.explanation: Support given within this zone is called scaffolding.

items.question: What is Bowlby's term for the strong emotional bond between an infant and its caregiver?
items.explanation: Bowlby argued that attachment is innate and has evolved to keep infants safe.

items.question: What is the name of Ainsworth's laboratory procedure used to classify an infant's attachment type?
items.explanation: The infant is observed during separations from and reunions with the caregiver.

items.text: Ainsworth's attachment type in which the infant uses the caregiver as a safe base and is comforted on reunion is {{secure}} attachment.
items.explanation: The insecure types are avoidant and resistant (ambivalent).

items.question: Which model of health states that biological, psychological and social factors interact to determine health and illness?
items.explanation: It replaced the purely biomedical model of illness.

items.text: Selye's {{general adaptation syndrome}} describes the stress response in three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion.
items.explanation: Prolonged stress leads to the exhaustion stage and illness.

items.question: Which model states that people's health behaviour depends on their perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers?
items.explanation: It is used to predict behaviours such as vaccination or quitting smoking.

items.question: What is the name of the manual published by the American Psychiatric Association used to diagnose mental disorders?
items.explanation: The WHO's ICD is the main alternative classification system.

items.question: What is the term for the proportion of a population that has a disorder at a given point in time?
items.explanation: Incidence, in contrast, counts new cases over a period of time.

items.question: Which therapy, developed by Beck, treats disorders such as depression by changing maladaptive thoughts and behaviours?
items.explanation: CBT is a first-line treatment for depression and anxiety disorders.

items.text: According to Lazarus and Folkman, coping that aims to remove or reduce the stressor itself is {{problem-focused}} coping.
items.explanation: Emotion-focused coping manages feelings about the stressor instead.

items.question: Who conducted the 1963 obedience experiment in which participants believed they were giving electric shocks to a learner?
items.explanation: The study was designed to test whether ordinary people would obey orders to harm others.

items.question: In Milgram's 1963 obedience study, what percentage of participants continued to the maximum 450-volt shock?
items.explanation: 26 out of 40 participants obeyed to the end.

items.question: In Milgram's obedience study, who was the 'learner' who appeared to receive the shocks?
items.explanation: No real shocks were given; the learner's cries were pre-recorded.

items.question: Who conducted the 1951 conformity study in which participants judged the lengths of lines?
items.explanation: The task was easy; conformity came from group pressure, not difficulty.

items.text: In Asch's 1951 study, the other 'participants' were {{confederates}} instructed to give the same wrong answer.
items.explanation: On critical trials, the naive participant answered after hearing the group's wrong answers.

items.question: In Asch's 1951 conformity study, roughly what proportion of participants conformed to the wrong answer at least once?
items.explanation: Overall, participants conformed on about a third of the critical trials.

items.question: In Loftus and Palmer's 1974 study, which verb in the question about the car crash produced the highest speed estimates?
items.explanation: 'Smashed' gave about 41 mph on average, 'contacted' about 32 mph.

items.question: Loftus and Palmer (1974) showed that memory can be distorted by the wording of questions asked after an event. What is this effect called?
items.explanation: This has important implications for eyewitness testimony.

items.question: In Loftus and Palmer's second experiment (1974), participants who heard the verb 'smashed' were more likely to falsely report seeing what?
items.explanation: There was no broken glass in the film, showing that memory was reconstructed.

items.question: In Bandura's 1961 study, children watched an adult attack which toy?
items.explanation: Children who saw the aggressive model later imitated the same aggressive acts.

items.question: What did Bandura's Bobo doll study (1961) demonstrate as a way children acquire aggressive behaviour?
items.explanation: It supports social learning theory: behaviour can be learned without direct reinforcement.

items.question: Patient HM lost the ability to form new long-term memories after surgery removed most of which brain structure?
items.explanation: The surgery in 1953 was intended to treat his severe epilepsy.

items.text: After his surgery, patient HM could not form new long-term memories; this type of memory loss is called {{anterograde}} amnesia.
items.explanation: His memories from before the surgery were largely intact.

items.question: HM could learn new motor skills such as mirror drawing but could not remember practising them. Which kind of memory was therefore intact?
items.explanation: This showed that explicit and procedural memory depend on different brain systems.

items.question: At which university did Zimbardo run his 1971 prison simulation study?
items.explanation: The study was stopped after six days instead of the planned two weeks.

items.question: Zimbardo's prison study was planned to last two weeks. After how many days was it stopped?
items.explanation: Guards became abusive and prisoners showed severe distress.

items.text: The six key concepts of the DP psychology course are bias, causality, change, {{measurement}}, perspective and responsibility.
items.explanation: The concepts run through all content and contexts and are assessed in the exam papers.

items.question: What form does the internal assessment take in the DP psychology course (first assessment 2027)?
items.explanation: Students design a study on a topic of interest instead of running a simple experiment.
